anti_overlap: fd-japanese-joinery-structural-trust covers element connections. fd-ottoman-calligraphy-visual-hierarchy covers visual proportion. fd-swiss-watchmaking-precision-tolerance covers timing precision.
decision_lens: Does the page create a spatial-emotional sequence that moves the visitor through distinct psychological states toward a moment of commitment, or does it present all elements simultaneously?
distance_rationale: Medieval sacred architecture was designed to produce spiritual experiences through physical space — a stone-and-light discipline with no concept of digital interfaces or conversion metrics.
expected_isomorphisms: Both cathedrals and landing pages must move a person through psychological states toward commitment using spatial arrangement alone. The principle that the altar should not be visible from the doorway maps to whether a landing page reveals its ask too early.
focus: Whether the page creates a spatial narrative that moves the visitor through a deliberate experiential sequence from threshold to commitment
name: fd-wayfinding-cathedral-spatial-progression
persona: An architectural historian specializing in medieval European cathedral design and liturgical spatial programming — specifically the choreography of processional movement from narthex through nave to crossing to sanctuary.
review_areas: Whether the nav functions as a proper narthex (threshold) — establishing context and orientation before the visitor enters the page's interior.
Whether the headline-to-animation sequence creates the nave experience — sufficient 'approach' that builds anticipation before the conversion ask.
Whether the diff animation functions as the crossing — the pivot point where attention is redirected from observation to desire.
Whether the form placement creates altar intimacy — appropriate scale compression after the larger demonstration space.
Whether there is a labyrinth — an alternative path for visitors not ready for direct approach (secondary CTA, social link, bookmark-worthy element).

severity_examples.condition: When the only interactive endpoint on the page is the waitlist form, and no mechanism exists to capture partial interest
severity_examples.scenario: No alternative path for visitors who are interested but not ready to commit — no secondary CTA, no social link, no content to bookmark.

severity_examples.condition: When the waitlist form is visible in the initial viewport on standard desktop resolutions without scrolling
severity_examples.scenario: The form appears within immediate scroll of the headline — the altar is visible from the narthex with insufficient spatial progression.

severity_examples.condition: When the post-submission state contains only a confirmation message with no onboarding content or next step
severity_examples.scenario: The success state provides no post-commitment experience — no ambulatory behind the altar.

source_domain: Medieval European cathedral architecture, specifically liturgical spatial programming from the Romanesque-Gothic tradition
success_hints: The page creates a felt progression through distinct psychological states: orientation, demonstration, desire, and commitment — with each state occupying its correct spatial position. Visitors not ready to commit have an alternative path. The post-commitment space rewards the act of joining.
task_context: Single-screen layout: LandingNav at top, then centered column (max-w-2xl) with pt-[12vh] containing headline → LandingHero → WaitlistForm, plus hidden ThemeSwitcher. On desktop, the entire page likely fits in a single viewport. No secondary CTA, no blog link, no social proof section. Success state replaces the form with confirmation text and a share button.
